newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila firms turn to Chinese corn due to shortage.
newsitem.headline: Manila firms turn to Chinese corn due to shortage.

text.p: Philippine poultry and hog firms have turned to Chinese corn to ease a local shortage, traders and industry officials said.
"Everybody's screaming for more corn," a senior Manila grains trader told Reuters.
The trader said Philippine feed millers, hog and poultry firms have bought between 80,000 and 95,000 tonnes of corn for July arrival since June 2.
"Last week, Philippine firms turned to Chinese corn to ensure that the commodity will arrive in the country in 10 to 15 days," an executive in a Philippine feed mill told Reuters.

Philippine firms prefer either U.S. or Argentina corn because of its high quality, company executives told Reuters. "But shipping time from the U.S. takes a month so most firms rushed to China to meet short term requirements."

Feeds and poultry firm Vitarich Corp was looking for 8,000 tonnes of Chinese corn for July delivery, traders said. Last week, Swift Foods Inc bought 10,000 tonnes of Chinese corn at $138 per tonne C&F for July arrival.
A group of hog raisers also bought 15,000 tonnes corn at $138 to $140 per tonne C&F for July arrival.
On June 2, a group of Philippine feed millers and hog raisers bought 55,000 tonnes U.S. corn at $137.75 per tonne C&F.

Besides high prices of domestic corn due to a local shortage, Philippine firms are rushing to the import market for corn due to a drop in tariff on the commodity from 100 percent to 80 percent starting July 1.
The tariff cut on corn imports will be implemented as part of Manila's commitment to the World Trade Organisation.
A lower tariff of 35 percent is slapped if the corn is imported through the state-owned National Food Authority but this was barred by a Philippine corn early this month.

A group representing farmers and traders had protested against lower tariff on commodities including corn, frozen beef, poultry, pork, and sugar imported under the government's minimum access volume (MAV) saying it discriminated against new entrants.
But traders said that even at 80 percent tariff, imported corn is cheaper than domestic corn.
"At $138 per tonne, the landed cost of imported corn is 7.14 pesos per kg," said Edward Acosta, vice president for the feeds division of Swift.
Traders said the wholesale price of domestic corn is now pegged between eight pesos to 10 pesos per kg.
Philippine hog and poultry farmers had asked the NFA to import 300,000 tonnes of corn before July.
"But because of the court order, we may have to import on our own," an executive in a Philippine mill said.
Philippine hog raisers said the domestic corn shortage may reach between one to two million tonnes this year.
Agriculture Secretary Salvador Escudero had said the Philippines may likely import 500,000 tonnes of corn this year.
The Philippines has so far imported between 230,000 and 245,000 tonnes of corn.

Traders said they expected a lull in corn imports in August. Philippine importers may likely be in the market again either September or October on prospects of a 10 to 15 percent drop in U.S. or Chinese corn because of a new corn crop.
